body: Continual pre-training (CPT) is a standard route for domain adaptation, yet existing studies typically track pre-training loss or multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) accuracy alone, offering only a narrow view of how adaptation unfolds. We jointly track factual knowledge via MCQA and open-ended behavior via pairwise preference rankings across 18 checkpoints for each of eight instruction-tuned Qwen models (0.5B to 8B), adapted to German medicine with CPT and SLERP merging. The two axes converge at consistently different rates, with preference rankings reaching 90% of their total gain after a median of 1.7B tokens versus 3.5B for MCQA. A judge-free token-distribution measure reaches this threshold at 1.9B tokens. Per-aspect scores indicate that these early preference gains largely reflect surface alignment, meaning models can sound domain-appropriate before their factual knowledge catches up. Larger adapted models close more of the gap to unadapted next-tier generalists, whereas preference gain per FLOP falls by about an order of magnitude across our size range. We therefore argue that judge-based preference scores, which can plateau while MCQA knowledge is still improving, should not be used alone to infer adaptation convergence or domain readiness.
